Historically it was useful in using static hosts and dynamic hosts in related pools, but that's not been a reality of our deployment recently. This deprecation and warning is the first step in this process.

Sb) / min(Sa, Sb) -1. For example for 3 / 1 it will give 2 (or 200%), for 1 /3 it will give -2 (or -200%), for 1 / 1 it will give 0(%). title: write new host allocator
description: The current host allocator (duration-based) is too complex (as it accounts for hosts to appear in multiple distros) but we should be able to write a drop-in replacement that allocates hosts based on the expected runtime of tasks, with some adjustments.    We've observed a number of cases where the scheduler *over* allocates hosts and they end up being terminated because the queue is empty by the time they have started.     I think we should make the following adjustments:     - currently evergreen assumes that tasks without past runtimes have runtimes of 10 minutes. I think there are enough tasks in the system that are shorter than 10 minutes, that we should change this assumption to 5m or 2m30s. We could also compute an average runtime for *all* tasks in the system (project?) and just use that.   - we should never allocate *more* than the total number of pending tasks in the queue. (and probably allocate somewhat less.)   - allocate enough hosts to run the tasks in the queue in the specified time. (this is what we mostly do now.    More details to come.

title: agent package should not depend on database methods.
description: this should probably be broken up into parts including:   - write a linter to enforce this  - moving some easier roues from the legacy routes to restv2 (depends on restv2 being able to do host-check)   - mirroring some types to apimodels.  - cleaning up the client.Communicator interface to not depend on models either to avoid a transitive leak.     Why?   - the interface contract between api server is to easy to break across agent upgrade versions.   - if the agent were much simpler we could deploy it only when it changed (and go back to having more than one binary, but if the agent didn't have the entire world, that might be better.)   - most of the agent's stability is due to human vigilance and specific humans keeping a look out for slip ups, which is a bad QA strategy. Keeping more details out of human's brains is good.
